text.gross: Diffuse flattening of gyri and narrowed sulci; brain may herniate
text.histo: Vasogenic: extracellular white matter fluid; cytotoxic: swollen cells
text.why: BBB disruption or ATP-dependent pump failure
text.notes:
Two types: Cytotoxic edema and vasogenic

Cytotoxic edema:
Accumulation of fluid intracellularly in astrocytes, endothelial cells, neurons, and
oligodendrocytes
• Secondary to altered cellular metabolism
• Interference with Na+/K+-ATPase pump
• Can’t maintain cellular homeostasis
• Results in elevated intracellular sodium and thus influx of water
• Blood-brain barrier remains intact
• Causes of cytotoxic edema:
• Hypoxia-ischemia
• Severe hypothermia
• Some toxicants

Vasogenic edema:
Most common type of edema in the CNS
• Occurs after vascular injury adjacent to inflammation, hematomas, contusions,
infarcts, cerebral hypertension, or neoplasms
• An increase in vascular permeability from the breakdown of the blood-brain barrier
• Allows movement of plasma constituents (water, ions, plasma proteins) into the extracellular
space
• Can be accompanied by some cellular
 swelling involving astrocytes
• Increases intracranial pressure
• If severe, pressure can cause neurologic
 dysfunction and caudal displacement of
 brain structures
(ie. coning of the cerebellar vermis)

text.gross: Yellow-white soft focal lesion compressing surrounding brain
text.histo: Necrotic neutrophilic focus with reactive gliosis
text.why: Can cause mass effect; fibrous capsules may be poorly developed in CNS
text.notes:
Sequelae: Depending on size and location,
can compress/displace tissue and/or vital
structures (ex: cardiac or respiratory centers)

text.gross: Gross and clinical consequence: Inflammation in epaxial musculature may extend dorsolaterally and compress the spinal cord.
text.dx: Working identification: Vertebral abscess. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Gross and clinical consequence: Inflammation in epaxial musculature may extend dorsolaterally and compress the spinal cord. Do not confuse: An extrinsic compressive abscess is different from primary inflammatory destruction of spinal cord parenchyma.
text.why: Origin: Often extension from vertebral osteomyelitis, discospondylitis or adjacent injury (the slides include tail docking); less commonly hematogenous. Do not confuse: An extrinsic compressive abscess is different from primary inflammatory destruction of spinal cord parenchyma.

text.gross: Cloudy yellow-white exudate along meninges and sulci
text.histo: Neutrophils and fibrin in subarachnoid space
text.why: Bacteremia; distinguish meningitis from parenchymal encephalitis

photos.caption: Marked vasculitis and vascular necrosis, thrombosis/ infarction

text.gross:
Randomly scattered, irregularly sized foci of hemorrhage and necrosis; cerebral edema. 
Mostly in the cerebrum, common at the*** cortical grey-white matter interface ***
+/- leptomeningitis with cloudiness of the CSF
text.dx:
Brain: multifocal hemorrhagic necrotizing thrombotic meningoencephalitis
Most frequent in the cerebrum, commonly on the *grey-white matter interface*
Etiology: ***Histophilus somi ***
text.histo: Marked vasculitis and vascular necrosis, thrombosis/ infarcation.
text.why: Histophilus somni enters the respiratory tract--> bacterial proliferation--> hematogenous spread to the CNS--> direct damage to endothelial cells --> thrombosis, necrosis, inflammation.
text.notes:
***Histophilus somni*** endothelial injury which results in septicemia in cattle.
Variable clinical presentations, including pneumonia, polyarthritis, myocarditis, abortion, and meningoencephalitis
• Most prevalent in feedlot cattle, typically 6 – 12 months of age  
**C/S:** Initial ataxia and circling, head pressing, and appear to be blind.

pathx-68-9.title: Overeating disease — C. perfringens type D

text.gross: Gross: Often no visible lesion. When present, bilateral symmetric yellow/gray/red foci of malacia and cavitation preferentially in white matter. Do not confuse: Symmetric toxin-associated white matter lesions versus random septic embolic lesions from TME.
text.dx: **Working identification: **Overeating disease — ***C. perfringens type D.*** Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: No distinctive histologic pattern is specified in this lecture section. Do not infer an organism or cell type from gross morphology alone.
text.why:
**Species and trigger:** Sheep and goats of any age after sudden* diet* change causing microbial imbalance and clostridial proliferation. 
**Why CNS damage occurs: **Enterotoxemia produces vascular injury and breakdown of the blood-brain barrier.

text.gross: Often no gross visible mass; when present, irregular gray-white to red, gelatinous/granular foci in white matter, especially brainstem. Can have a gelatinous or granular consistency.
text.dx:
Working identification: Granulomatous meningoencephalitis (GME). 
Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord/meninges. 
Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity, and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Perivascular cuffs containing macrophages and lymphocytes with relatively few plasma cells.
text.why:
**Idiopathic condition. **
**Host: **Young to middle-aged small-breed dogs, idiopathic with suspected T-cell-mediated mechanism.
 Differentiate: GME perivascular inflammation from the suppurative microabscesses of Listeria or thrombotic lesions of Histophilus.
text.notes:
Most severe in the brainstem (white matter) 
**Clinical:** Behavior change, circling, seizures; paresis and ataxia when spinal cord is involved. 

**Differentiate:** GME perivascular inflammation from the suppurative microabscesses of Listeria or thrombotic lesions of *Histophilus.*

text.gross: Irreversibly injured neurons may not create a visible gross lesion early
text.histo: Angular shrunken intensely eosinophilic ( hypereosinophilic) red neurons with pyknotic or lost nuclei
text.why: Ischemia/ATP failure or other neuronal injury; distinguish normal neurons from injured red neurons. Common response to a variety of CNS injuries.
text.notes: Neurons are the most susceptible of CNS cells to ischemia (neurons> oligodendrocytes> astrocytes> microglia> endothelial cells)

text.gross:
Well-demarcated focal regional softening (malacia), swelling or hemorrhagic discoloration depending on timing/
**Grey Matter: ** hemorrhagic 
**White Matter: ** often pale. 
Small (<1mm) areas filled with astrocytes on histo, larger ones can become cyst like
text.histo:
Neuronal necrosis and later macrophage infiltration with tissue rarefaction
areas will be filled with astrocytes
text.why:
Blood flow failure causes energy depletion and necrosis; distribution follows vessel.
More rapid ischemia → more severe lesion
• Sudden obstruction (ex: embolus, compression) → neurons die
within minutes
• Gradual reduction in flow (ex: atherosclerosis) → often
sufficient time for anastomotic vessels to dilate and
compensate
text.notes: Necrosis in the CNS is liquefactive.

text.gross:
Granular, gray-white plexus with hyperemia/hemorrhage and cloudy to yellow-green, thick or gelatinous in the ventricular system. 
Choroid plexuses may be granular and gray/ white with hyperemia and hemorrhage. 
Why it matters: Inflammation may extend through CSF spaces into the leptomeninges, and purulent exudate can impede CSF flow, causing acquired hydrocephalus.
text.dx: Working identification: Choroid plexitis. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Location: Inflammation of the choroid plexus, most commonly due to bacteria entering directly or hematogenously, though viral infection is possible. Why it matters: Inflammation may extend through CSF spaces into the leptomeninges, and purulent exudate can impede CSF flow, causing acquired hydrocephalus.
text.why: Why it matters: Inflammation may extend through CSF spaces into leptomeninges, and purulent exudate can impede CSF flow, causing acquired hydrocephalus. Differentiate: Choroid plexus is the CSF-producing structure; ependyma lines the ventricular wall.
text.notes:
If severe, it can traverse the fourth ventricle and spread throughout the subarachnoid space, causing suppurative leptomeningitis. The exudate can also obstruct the CSF flow *which can lead to hydrocephalus. *

Also called Ependymitis.

text.gross: Opaque, hyperemic meninges (typically referring to leptomeninges) with yellow-white exudate tracking sulci; distinguish inflammation of pia/arachnoid and subarachnoid space from thickened inflamed dura.
text.dx: CNS meninges: diffuse fibrinosuppurative leptomeningitis (working pattern; etiology pending)
text.histo: Suppurative leptomeningitis: abundant neutrophils/fibrin within the subarachnoid space. Nonsuppurative: lymphocytes/mononuclear cells. Granulomatous: macrophages/giant cells and possible fungi. Pachymeningitis: dura. Meningoencephalitis: adjacent brain parenchyma.
text.why:
Septicemia or contiguous infection can seed the meninges; gross appearance and leukocyte pattern localize and classify inflammation, but bacterial identity requires laboratory confirmation. Can be spread by direct extension or leukocyte trafficking. 
Most commonly caused by bacteria that reach the leptomeninges and subarachnoid space** hematogenously. **
text.notes:
Strict viral leptomeningitis is rare (those tend to cause meningoencephalitis)
Can have multiple levels of chronicitiy.

text.gross:
Firm white-tan granulomas/pyogranulomas; fibrin-rich ventricular exudate, white to tan plaques along sulci or near circle of Willis. 
Secondary: Ventricular exudate can cause hydrocephalus or cerebellar herniation.
text.dx: Working identification: Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) CNS disease. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo:
Pyogranulomatous nodules with vasculitis
Tends to perfer involvement to small to medium-sized veins.
text.why: Cause/pathogenesis: Feline coronavirus-associated disease with macrophage replication and dissemination. Secondary: Ventricular exudate can cause hydrocephalus or cerebellar herniation.
text.notes: CNS C/S: Behavorial changes, dullness, coma, paresis, ataxis, paralysis and seizures.

pathx-68-25.title: Fungal CNS infections — overview and differential etiologies

text.gross: Moderately well demarcated, expansive, yellow- brown foci that displace and disrupt normal tissue.
text.dx:
Most cases are opportunistic infections in immunocompromised individuals. 
Aspergillus is an example of trophism for vessels (angioinvasive) and can cause vasculitis leading to thrombosis or infarction. 

**Working identification:** Fungal CNS infections — overview and differential etiologies. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord/meninges.
text.histo:
Granulomatous to pyogranulomatous inflammation with spores able to be seen in samples. 
Can have angioinvasive with vessel trophism species.
text.why: **Fungal agents in professor's list:** *Aspergillus, Candida, Cryptococcus neoformans, the historical 'Zygomycetes' group, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Histoplasma capsulatum and Coccidioides spp. *

text.gross: Cloudy/viscous leptomeninges and multiple small cyst-like lesions with a viscous, *gelatinous* appearance of the meninges or CNS parenchyma.
text.dx:
Working identification:* Cryptococcosis — C. neoformans / C. gattii*. 
Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
*Cryptococcus spp. secrete a thick complex polysaccharide capsule that protects the fungus from host defenses*
text.histo: Encapsulated budding yeasts, often with a prominent clear halo around the organism; inflammation varies with host immune response. Confirm with microbiology.
text.why: Hosts: Particular CNS affinity in cats and dogs, occasionally horses.
text.notes:
**Diagnostic confirmation:** Evaluate tissue cytology/histology and organism identification; fungal antigen testing can support cryptococcosis. A gross lesion alone does not prove etiology.
**Route of infection:**
• Enters the leptomeninges by direct extension through the
cribriform plate after a nasal or sinus infection
• Hematogenous usually from a pulmonary infection.
• Spread of the infection can result in encephalitis and ventriculitis

Immunosuppression (i.e viral infections or long term
glucocorticoid) can increase susceptibility
• Immunocompetent animals usually clear the infection before it spreads systemically

text.gross:
Hemorrhage or necrosis; *multifocal necrosis with glial nodules and mixed inflammation*; yellow-brown-gray granular foci in gray or white matter. 
**Chronic: **Larger granular discolored areas may blur gray-white boundaries.
text.dx:
Working identification: Neosporosis — Neospora caninum. Affinity for the nervous system. 
**Transmission:** Ingestion of cysts or transplacental infection 
Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord/meninges. 
Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Can see oocysts, tachyzoites, or bradyzoites, depending on the stage, which aids in chronicity.
text.why:
**Host and transmission:** Dogs, cattle and other mammals; infection can follow ingestion of cysts or transplacental spread. 
**Age differences**: Young dogs: polyradiculoneuritis/polymyositis; adult dogs: encephalitis (often cerebellum) and myositis.
text.notes:
Neurologic disease can be divided into two categories:
- Polyradiculoneuritis and polymyositis: young dogs
-Encephalitis (predilection for cerebellum_ and myosititis: adult dogs 
**Stages**
Oocysts (environmental stages formed in canine intestinal epithelium and passed with the feces)
Tachyzoites (asexual rapidly growing stages that actively invade tissues; present during acute phase of infection.

Bradyzoites (slowly dividing stages that encyst within tissues)

photo.caption: Lecture 68 · Toxoplasmosis (T. gondii) — review image ID

text.gross: No consistent gray-versus-white-matter predilection in the CNS. Focal hemorrhage and necrosis may develop into yellow-brown to gray, granular foci; spinal nerve roots may also be involved.
text.dx: Working identification: Toxoplasmosis due to Toxoplasma gondii. Specimen site: brain / spinal cord / meninges. For a morphologic diagnosis, specify the observed tissue and inflammation/necrosis pattern, distribution, and supported severity; the gross appearance alone cannot establish etiology.
text.histo: Protozoal infection can involve neurons and astrocytes with necrosis and associated hemorrhage/inflammation. The pattern and identification of organisms require histologic confirmation.
text.why: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular protozoan. Transplacental infection can affect the developing CNS. In mature animals, clinically apparent CNS disease may occur with immunosuppression, including concurrent canine distemper. Differentiate this protozoal disease from nematode larval migration by organism and lesion pattern.
text.notes:
This parasite targets different cell types. Parasitizes variety of cell types (lungs, lymphoid system, liver, heart, skeletal muscle, pancreas,
gastrointestinal (GI) tract, eyes, and nervous system)
• CNS infection targets neurons and astrocytes

In mature animals, T. gondii infections have been associated with immunosuppression, like canine distempter virus.
text.visualClue: Multifocal CNS hemorrhage/necrosis without a predictable preference for gray versus white matter; protozoal organisms may be found in neural tissue.
text.compare: Toxocara canis cerebrospinal larval migration: migrating nematode larvae can leave linear hemorrhagic/necrotic tracks and eosinophilic inflammation. Neosporosis: also protozoal, but distribution, affected animals, and muscle/nerve-root lesions can help distinguish.
text.zoonoticNotes: Zoonotic considerations require exposure-route guidance; CNS lesions in an animal alone do not establish transmission risk.

text.gross: Random, variably sized irregular dark-red/brown foci of hemorrhage/necrosis in spinal cord gray/white matter; if brain involved, tends toward brainstem. This
text.dx: Working identification: Equine protozoal myeloencephalitis (EPM). Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Necrosis, hemorrhage and mixed perivascular inflammatory cuffs, often including eosinophils; lecture specifies no vasculitis.
text.why:
**Agents:** *Sarcocystis neurona* (most common) and *Neospora hughesi.* Lecture relates S. neurona infective sporocysts to opossum feces; do not assign the same source to both agents. 
**Risk/signs:** Young adults, stress or immunocompromise; deficits depend on location and include ataxia, cranial nerve signs, dysphagia and asymmetric muscle atrophy.
text.notes:
Signalment: Young adult horses under stress or immunocompromised. 
Clinical signs: Depression, seizures, ataxia, facial nerve paralysis, paralysis of the
tongue, dysphagia, atrophy of the quadriceps and/or gluteal muscles etc
• Signs depend on where protozoa localizes
